plain_title: Schizophrenia-like symptoms, one to six months in
one_liner: The same symptoms as schizophrenia, lasting more than a month but less than six months. A 'wait and see' diagnosis.
in_simple_words: Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed when someone has the symptoms of schizophrenia (psychosis, disorganization, negative symptoms) that have lasted longer than a month but not yet six months. It's essentially a provisional label: about a third of people recover within six months and never meet criteria for schizophrenia; the rest go on to be diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder. The name sounds daunting, but it mainly means 'too early to tell', and treatment starts now rather than waiting.
what_it_can_feel_like: Four months of voices and fear. Then, slowly, they faded, and the diagnosis was never changed to schizophrenia. I'm one of the lucky third.
The word terrified me until the nurse explained it meant they were watching and hoping.
Starting treatment early, before anyone was sure what it was, is probably why I'm okay.
common_signs: Psychotic symptoms like those of schizophrenia
Lasting between one and six months
Often good functioning before onset and confusion during the episode
Diagnosis revised at six months: recovered, or schizophrenia, or schizoaffective disorder

myths_vs_facts.myth: Schizophreniform disorder is just early schizophrenia.
myths_vs_facts.fact: About a third of people recover within six months and don't develop schizophrenia. The label leaves that door open.

myths_vs_facts.myth: You should wait until six months to start treatment.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Early treatment improves outcomes. Treatment starts as soon as psychosis is recognized.

myths_vs_facts.myth: A diagnosis that changes means the doctors were wrong.
myths_vs_facts.fact: This diagnosis is designed to change. It's honest about uncertainty.

how_common.plain: Schizophreniform disorder is uncommon, with lifetime rates estimated at around 1 in 500 in higher-income countries.
how_common.figure: Lifetime prevalence about 0.2% (DSM-5-TR text, higher-income countries)

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment is the same as for a first episode of psychosis: early intervention services, antipsychotic medication prescribed and monitored by a doctor, CBT for psychosis, family involvement, and support to stay in work or study. Close follow-up around the six-month mark decides what happens next. Good early functioning, confusion during the episode, and quick onset predict a better outcome.
evidence_based_options: Antipsychotic medication, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
CBT for psychosis and family intervention
Regular review and support with work or study
self_help_that_supports_care: Keeping connected to people, even when withdrawing feels easier
Learning early warning signs with your team
Peer support with others who've been through a first episode

when_to_reach_out: If psychotic symptoms have lasted more than a month, make sure you're linked to a mental health team, ideally an early intervention service. If you're in crisis or danger, use the crisis strip now.
is_not: Psychosis under a month is brief psychotic disorder; over six months, schizophrenia. Psychosis caused by drugs, medication, or a medical condition is diagnosed separately.
hope_note: A third of people with this diagnosis recover fully within months. For the rest, early treatment makes the road ahead much smoother.
